title: In Large Groups, Someone Will Always Be Offended
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This essay addresses the growing caution leaders feel about speaking candidly to large internal audiences, given how differently people now filter comments through strongly held personal and political beliefs. It observes that some leaders, burned by past pushback, retreat into only mundane comments or avoid open forums altogether, which the piece frames as a real cost to organizational transparency. Its central argument draws a parallel to how leaders already handle unpopular decisions -- they act in the organization's best interest despite knowing not everyone will agree -- and argues the same posture should apply to open communication: presume someone will take offense, accept that as unavoidable, and speak candidly anyway within clear bounds of appropriateness.
points: Audiences now filter what leaders say through strongly held social, political, and personal beliefs more than in the past.
Some leaders, burned by past audience pushback, retreat into only mundane comments or avoid open forums entirely.
This avoidance robs the broader audience of transparency and direct insight from the leader, which most organizations claim to value.
The essay draws a parallel to unpopular decisions: leaders accept that not everyone will agree and act anyway, and should apply the same posture to open speaking.
The recommended stance is to presume someone will find offense, accept that as unavoidable, and still communicate openly within clear bounds of appropriateness.
quotes: Strongly held social, political, and personal beliefs color what is heard and how people react.
This makes speaking to large groups, even inside the organization, dicey for leaders.
Given that someone is likely to accuse them of bad or biased intentions, the safest path may be to refrain from speaking at all.
Good leaders do what is in the best interest of the organization, team, and customers. Not everyone is going to agree with or like many of the decisions they make.
It is best to presume someone in any audience, maybe even a small group of people, will find offense in what is said or discussed.
The truth is, people can take offense to anything. There are no restrictions on how people can interpret what they hear.
